title: Infra playbook: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, Terraform modules, CI/CD and runbooks (consolidated v2)
author: Samantha Li
content:
Executive summary:
This v2 consolidated playbook captures the infra team's operational standards for GPU fleet capacity, cloud account and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipelines for infra code, and the primary runbooks used during incidents. It consolidates prior playbooks and adds updated CI gating and emergency expansion procedures.

Intended audience:
- Infra engineers, SREs, compute-platform, and on-call responders.

Document owner & contacts:
- Owner: infra-team@redwood.ai (Infra Engineering)
- On-call rotation: infra-oncall@redwood.ai (see PagerDuty schedule)
- Escalation: compute-platform@redwood.ai -> security@redwood.ai (if cross-account/networking impact)

High-level architecture and fleet segmentation:
- production-gpu-pool: primary low-latency inference capacity (pinned models). SLO target: p95 request latency < 120ms.
- burst-gpu-pool: elastic capacity for traffic spikes and large batched jobs (non-latency workloads).
- staging-gpu-pool: pre-prod validation and canaries.
- perf-gpu-pool: kernels, benchmarking, and perf regression testing.
- pools are implemented as separate ASGs / VMSS / managed node groups per region and account to enforce isolation and billing.

Cloud accounts & networking patterns:
- Account model: one cloud account per environment (prod/staging/dev) plus per-customer dedicated accounts for Private deployments.
- Ownership: infra owns the account bootstrap; security approves guardrails.
- VPC topology: hub-and-spoke. The hub contains shared services (bastion, logging, monitoring) and spoke VPCs contain GPU pools and dedicated workloads.
- Connectivity: use managed Transit Gateway or equivalent for cross-account routing; avoid manual peering unless temporary.
- Egress & NAT: centralized NAT gateways in the hub; use VPC endpoints for S3, Secrets Manager, and ECR.
- Network guardrails: deny-by-default security group baseline from module/networking_common. Implement WAF and DDoS protections for public ingress.

Terraform / IaC conventions and module policy:
- Repo layout: infra-modules/ (reusable modules), infra-live/{prod,staging,dev}/ (environment overlays).
- Module requirements: semver tag on release (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), documented variables, outputs, examples/, CHANGELOG.md, and tests/. All modules require at least one integration test.
- State backend: S3 bucket with server-side encryption + DynamoDB lock table per environment. Access via IAM assume-role with MFA enforced for sensitive changes.
- Secrets: do not store secrets in state; use Secrets Manager or Vault and reference via data sources.
- Naming policy: resource names follow: r-<component>-<env>-<region>-<shortid>. Use tags: Team, Environment, CostCenter, Owner.
- Module lifecycle: breaking changes must include migration guide and automated migration plan.

Core modules (examples):
- module/gpu_cluster: manages node pools, AMI/AMI builder integration, instance families, autoscaling policy, and lifecycle hooks.
- module/networking_hub: VPC hub, route tables, NAT, Transit attachments, peering automation.
- module/cloud_account_bootstrap: baseline IAM roles, SCPs, logging, and monitoring onboarding.
- module/k8s_node_pool: node group, taints/labels, kubelet config, and kube-proxy tuning.
- module/monitoring_agent: logging + metrics agent deployment with default config for GPU hosts.

Example usage (Terraform snippet):
```
module "gpu_cluster" {
  source            = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu_cluster?ref=v1.4.1"
  name              = "prod-gpu-pool-usw2"
  environment       = "prod"
  region            = "us-west-2"
  instance_types    = ["p4d.24xlarge", "g5.12xlarge"]
  min_nodes         = 6
  desired_nodes     = 12
  max_nodes         = 250
  autoscaling_policy = "balanced"
  termination_protection = true
  tags = {
    Team = "inference"
    CostCenter = "prod-inference"
  }
}
```

CI/CD and pipeline standards (gating & execution):
- Where to run: short Terraform plans run in GitHub Actions; long-running applies or stateful migrations run in Jenkins with VTEX/maintenance windows.
- Preconditions: terraform fmt -> tflint -> tfsec -> terraform validate -> terraform plan. Policy checks (OPA/Rego) run after plan.
- Approvals: CODEOWNERS + infra-release approvers. Production apply requires a manual approval step and an attached runbook.
- Apply policy: automated apply allowed only for dev/staging. Production applies are run via a gated Jenkins job: job infra/prod-apply with required approvers and runbook link.
- Canary & rollout policy: changes touching autoscaler, instance families, or kernel parameters must follow canary path: staging -> perf-gpu-pool -> small prod shard -> global. Keep canary windows at least 24 hours with perf metrics.

Testing strategy & quality gates:
- Unit tests: static checks and module unit tests using terraform-compliance and local test harnesses.
- Integration tests: Terratest suites that deploy minimal infra into ephemeral test accounts; tests must complete under 30m where possible.
- Policy-as-code: enforce using Conftest/OPA; deny IAM policies with overly permissive statements and unencrypted S3 buckets.
- Post-apply smoke tests: ensure nodes join cluster, metrics pipeline emits GPU metrics, and a sample inference pod can start.

Capacity planning, SLOs, and headroom policy:
- Target steady-state utilization: 60% average across 1-week window.
- Alerting thresholds:
  - Warning: 95p utilization > 65% for 30m
  - Critical: 95p utilization > 80% for 15m -> trigger P1 page.
- Scale logic: scale-up when 95p > 75% for 30m; scale-down when average < 40% sustained for 6h and pending pods = 0.
- Headroom policy: keep 15% spare capacity and pre-warm nodes during known traffic windows.
- Cost controls: use spot instances for burst-pool where acceptable; run batch jobs in preemptible windows and prefer quantized instance variants for low-cost runs.

Runbook: GPU capacity exhaustion (detailed)
1) Detection:
   - Alerts: infra.capacity.gpu_pool_high_util (critical) and infra.pending.pods_high (warning). Check Grafana dashboard "GPU Fleet Capacity".
2) Triage (first responder):
   - Review recent ASG events, node provisioning failures, and cloud provider quota limits.
   - Run: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | grep Pending and oc get nodes -o wide.
3) Mitigation actions:
   - Supply-side issue: check cloud provider health and ASG errors. If nodes failing to join, restart the provisioning pipeline (infra/provision-nodes job) and follow node onboarding runbook.
   - Demand-side issue: temporarily shift non-critical routes to burst-gpu-pool via service routing rules in Smart Router or increase ASG max via infra admin pipeline.
   - Emergency expansion: run the Jenkins job infra/emergency-expand with 2 approvers from infra-oncall and compute-platform. Document change and notify on Incident channel.
4) Recovery and post-incident:
   - Reconcile scaling activity, review why autoscaler didn't provision in time, and tune cooled-down timers or max limits.
   - Create incident postmortem and action items assigned in the incident backlog.

Runbook: GPU host node failure
- Symptoms: node NotReady, kubelet errors, kernel oops in serial logs, SIGQUIT in host logs.
- Steps:
  1) Identify node: kubectl describe node <node> and check cloud console for instance status.
  2) If transient: cordon + drain: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force; then trigger reprovision.
  3) If persistent (hardware): mark instance family as suspect, failover workloads to alternate families, open provider support ticket, and notify compute-platform and purchasing for RMA tracking.
  4) After recovery: check kernel versions, nv driver versions, and AMI patch levels; add test cases to perf pool where relevant.

Operational playbook: Changing autoscaling policy in prod
1) Author change in branch, include rationale and impact matrix in PR.
2) Run full pre-commit checks and Terratest locally.
3) Apply in staging and perf pools; run 24h perf collection (p95 latency, pod scheduling latency, pending pods).
4) Book maintenance window and obtain manual approvals (Infra owner, SRE lead, Product impact owner).
5) Execute prod apply via infra/prod-apply job and monitor metrics for 2 hours.

Monitoring, dashboards and alerts (practical examples):
- Dashboards: GPU Fleet Capacity, Node Lifecycle, Pending Pods by Queue, ASG Activity, Cost per Pool.
- Example Prometheus rules (simplified):
  - infra.capacity.gpu_pool_high_util -> expr: quantile_over_time(0.95, gpu_utilization[15m]) > 0.8
  - infra.node.provision_failure -> expr: increase(node_provision_failures[30m]) > 3
- Pager severity: P1 (production outage or capacity critical), P2 (degraded performance), P3 (informational / tuning).

Best practices checklist (operational hygiene):
- Use modules; avoid ad-hoc resources in prod accounts.
- Keep AMI and driver versions consistent across region/instance families.
- Maintain module tests and example usage.
- Tag resources for cost attribution and ownership.
- Use canary rollouts for infra changes that affect pod scheduling or autoscaling.

CLI & helper snippets (quick reference):
- GPU utilization (PromQL): sum by(instance) (rate(nvidia_gpu_utilization[5m]))
- Drain node: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- Terraform plan for prod: TF_VAR_env=prod terraform plan -var-file=envs/prod.tfvars -out=prod.plan
- Apply (production gated): jenkins job infra/prod-apply -> upload prod.plan -> require 2 approvers

Quick reference table:
- Minimum prod nodes per region: 4 (recommended foothold 6 for high-availability)
- Default instance families: p4d, g5, a100 (region-dependent; prefer p4d for large models)
- Default root disk: 1 TB NVMe; ephemeral storage sized per workload needs
- Remote state: s3://redwood-terraform-prod-backend (SSE-KMS) + DynamoDB lock table infra-terraform-locks
